      "title": "What is the Default maximumPoolSize for HikariCP in Spring Boot? Impact of Over-Setting Connection Pool Size",
      "content": "## Table of Contents[#](https://www.javathinking.com#table-of-contents)

## What is HikariCP?[#](https://www.javathinking.com#what-is-hikaricp)

HikariCP is a "zero-overhead" production-grade connection pool for Java. Developed by Brett Wooldridge, it is renowned for its speed, efficiency, and minimal resource footprint. Spring Boot adopted HikariCP as the default connection pool in version 2.0 (replacing Tomcat JDBC Pool) due to its superior performance metrics, including:

- **Low latency**: Optimized connection retrieval and release logic.
- **Small codebase**: \~130KB JAR size, reducing startup time and memory overhead.
- **Smart pooling**: Features like adaptive timeout handling and connection health checks.

HikariCP's design philosophy emphasizes "doing more with less," making it ideal for high-throughput Spring Boot applications. Central to its configuration is `maximumPoolSize`, which dictates the upper limit of concurrent database connections the pool will manage.

## Default `maximumPoolSize` in Spring Boot: A Version-Specific Breakdown[#](https://www.javathinking.com#default-maximumpoolsize-in-spring-boot-a-version-specific-breakdown)

The default value of `maximumPoolSize` in HikariCP has remained consistent across Spring Boot versions. Understanding this default is critical for proper connection pool tuning.

### 1. Spring Boot \< 2.3: Fixed Default of 10 Connections[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-spring-boot-less-than-2-3-fixed-default-of-10-connections)

Prior to Spring Boot 2.3, HikariCP's `maximumPoolSize` was **fixed at 10 connections**, regardless of the underlying hardware (e.g., CPU cores, memory) or database capacity. This static default was a safe starting point but often required manual tuning for applications with high concurrency or running on multi-core servers.

### 2. Spring Boot ≥ 2.3: Default Remains at 10[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-spring-boot-2-3-default-remains-at-10)

Starting with Spring Boot 2.3, the default `maximumPoolSize` remains **fixed at 10 connections**, consistent with earlier versions. While Spring Boot 2.3 introduced many configuration improvements, it did not change the HikariCP default pool size from 10.

#### Why Not a Dynamic Default?[#](https://www.javathinking.com#why-not-a-dynamic-default)

Unlike some connection pool parameters that auto-tune based on hardware, `maximumPoolSize` requires careful consideration of your specific database server's capacity, not just CPU cores. A one-size-fits-all formula can be misleading—database workload characteristics (query complexity, connection holding time, etc.) vary significantly across applications.

#### Customizing Based on CPU Cores (Optional)[#](https://www.javathinking.com#customizing-based-on-cpu-cores-optional)

If you want to tune `maximumPoolSize` dynamically based on CPU cores, you can configure it manually in your `application.properties`:

This SpEL expression calculates `availableProcessors() * 2 + 1` at runtime. For example, on an 8-core CPU, this yields 17 connections.

#### Examples:[#](https://www.javathinking.com#examples)

- **4-core CPU**: `4 * 2 + 1 = 9` connections.
- **8-core CPU**: `8 * 2 + 1 = 17` connections.
- **16-core CPU**: `16 * 2 + 1 = 33` connections.

Use this approach only after verifying your database can handle the increased connection load.

## Why Does This Default Exist? The Rationale Behind the Heuristic[#](https://www.javathinking.com#why-does-this-default-exist-the-rationale-behind-the-heuristic)

The default of 10 connections in Spring Boot is not arbitrary. It is rooted in performance engineering principles and real-world database behavior:

### 1. Avoiding Database Overload[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-avoiding-database-overload)

Databases have finite resources (CPU, memory, I/O). Each connection consumes database memory (e.g., for session state, query caching) and can increase lock contention. Too many connections overwhelm the database, leading to slower query execution and timeouts.

### 2. Minimizing Thread Contention[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-minimizing-thread-contention)

Java threads (and thus database connections) compete for CPU time. Excessive connections lead to frequent context switching (the OS pausing one thread to run another), which degrades performance. The `availableProcessors() * 2 + 1` formula (if you choose to use it) aligns with the "optimal thread count" heuristic, where threads ≈ 2× CPU cores to keep cores busy without excessive switching.

### 3. Balancing Throughput and Latency[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-balancing-throughput-and-latency)

A pool that is too small causes request queuing and timeouts. Too large wastes resources on idle connections. The default of 10 strikes a balance: enough connections to handle typical workloads, but not so many that the database becomes a bottleneck.

## How to Verify the Default `maximumPoolSize`[#](https://www.javathinking.com#how-to-verify-the-default-maximumpoolsize)

To confirm the active `maximumPoolSize` in your Spring Boot application, use one of these methods:

### 1. Check HikariCP Startup Logs[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-check-hikaricp-startup-logs)

HikariCP logs pool configuration on startup. Look for a line like this in your application logs (adjust log level to `INFO` if needed):

Here, `maximumPoolSize=10` confirms the default pool size.

### 2. Programmatically Inspect the Pool[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-programmatically-inspect-the-pool)

Expose the `HikariDataSource` and log its configuration. Add this to a `@Configuration` class:

On startup, this will print the active `maximumPoolSize` to the console.

### 3. Use JMX[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-use-jmx)

HikariCP exposes metrics via JMX. Use tools like JConsole or VisualVM to connect to your application and navigate to `com.zaxxer.hikari:type=HikariPool (HikariPool-1)` → Attributes → `MaximumPoolSize`.

## Impact of Over-Setting `maximumPoolSize`: Risks and Consequences[#](https://www.javathinking.com#impact-of-over-setting-maximumpoolsize-risks-and-consequences)

It's tempting to increase `maximumPoolSize` to "handle more traffic," but this often backfires. Here's why over-setting the pool size harms performance:

### 1. Database Resource Starvation[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-database-resource-starvation)

Each connection consumes database resources (memory, file descriptors, locks). For example, PostgreSQL defaults to `max_connections=100`—if your app sets `maximumPoolSize=200`, the database will reject new connections, causing `SQLTransientConnectionException`.

### 2. Increased Context Switching[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-increased-context-switching)

Too many active connections mean more threads competing for CPU. The OS spends more time switching between threads than executing useful work, reducing throughput.

### 3. Connection Contention and Timeouts[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-connection-contention-and-timeouts)

Idle connections in an over-sized pool may become stale (due to database timeouts like `wait_timeout` in MySQL). When the pool tries to reuse them, it incurs reconnection overhead, leading to slower response times.

### 4. Wasted Memory[#](https://www.javathinking.com#4-wasted-memory)

Idle connections consume JVM memory (e.g., HikariCP's `idleTimeout` defaults to 600000ms/10 minutes). An over-sized pool wastes memory on unused connections, increasing GC pressure.

### 5. Masking Underlying Issues[#](https://www.javathinking.com#5-masking-underlying-issues)

A large pool can hide bottlenecks (e.g., slow queries, unoptimized indexes). Instead of fixing the root cause, you're papering over it with more connections, leading to unsustainable scaling.

### Example: The "Too Many Connections" Disaster[#](https://www.javathinking.com#example-the-too-many-connections-disaster)

An e-commerce app sets `maximumPoolSize=200` to handle Black Friday traffic. The database (with `max_connections=150`) starts rejecting connections. Retries exacerbate the issue, causing cascading failures. Meanwhile, the app's 200 threads spend most of their time waiting for database locks, dropping throughput by 40%.

## Best Practices for Setting `maximumPoolSize`[#](https://www.javathinking.com#best-practices-for-setting-maximumpoolsize)

Follow these steps to optimize `maximumPoolSize` for your workload:

### 1. Start with the Default[#](https://www.javathinking.com#1-start-with-the-default)

The default of 10 connections works for most applications. Only tune if you observe connection-related bottlenecks (e.g., `HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms`).

### 2. Monitor Pool Metrics[#](https://www.javathinking.com#2-monitor-pool-metrics)

Track these HikariCP metrics to identify issues:

- `ActiveConnections`: Number of in-use connections (should stay below `maximumPoolSize`).
- `IdleConnections`: Unused connections (high values indicate over-provisioning).
- `PendingConnections`: Requests waiting for a connection (high values mean the pool is too small).

Use tools like Micrometer + Prometheus/Grafana to visualize these metrics.

### 3. Respect Database Limits[#](https://www.javathinking.com#3-respect-database-limits)

Check your database's `max_connections` (e.g., `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections'` in MySQL). Set `maximumPoolSize` to **≤ (max\_connections - reserved\_connections)** (reserve connections for admins/other apps).

### 4. Load-Test Under Realistic Traffic[#](https://www.javathinking.com#4-load-test-under-realistic-traffic)

Simulate peak load with tools like JMeter. If `PendingConnections` spike, increment `maximumPoolSize` by small steps (e.g., +5) and retest. Stop when adding connections no longer improves throughput.

### 5. Tune Complementary Settings[#](https://www.javathinking.com#5-tune-complementary-settings)

- `connectionTimeout`: Time to wait for a connection (default: 30000ms). Increase if `PendingConnections` are high but the pool isn't saturated.
- `idleTimeout`: Time to keep idle connections (default: 600000ms). Reduce for memory-constrained environments.
- `minIdle`: Minimum idle connections (default: same as `maximumPoolSize`). Lower to free resources if idle connections are high.

## Conclusion[#](https://www.javathinking.com#conclusion)

HikariCP's `maximumPoolSize` is a critical lever for Spring Boot performance, but more is not better. Spring Boot's default of 10 connections provides a safe starting point that balances throughput and database health for most applications. Over-setting the pool size leads to database overload, context switching, and wasted resources.

Optimize `maximumPoolSize` by monitoring metrics, respecting database limits, and load-testing. When in doubt, start with the default and tune incrementally. Your database (and users) will thank you.",

      "title": "HikariCP Pool Size Guide: maximumPoolSize and minimumIdle",
      "content": "HikariCP pool size should be treated as a capacity control, not a performance score. maximumPoolSize sets the upper connection limit, while minimumIdle affects how many idle connections the pool tries to maintain when configured below that maximum.

## What maximumPoolSize changes

The pool maximum includes idle and in-use connections. When every connection is in use and the pool is at its maximum, new callers wait for a connection until one is returned or the connection timeout is reached.

A higher maximum can reduce queueing only if the database can productively handle the additional concurrent work.

## How minimumIdle affects behavior

minimumIdle asks the pool to maintain a baseline of idle connections. The HikariCP project documentation notes that leaving it unset can allow fixed-size behavior based on maximumPoolSize, which is a useful starting point for many workloads.

Do not set a large idle baseline without understanding database connection costs and infrastructure limits.

## Use database capacity as a boundary

The application is not the only client of the database. Administrators, background jobs, other services and maintenance tools may share the same connection limit. Reserve operational headroom instead of allocating every possible database connection to one pool.

## Include transaction duration in sizing

Long transactions keep connections checked out for longer periods, which increases the number of concurrent connections needed for the same request rate. Reducing transaction duration can be more effective than increasing the pool.

## Validate with load tests

Start from a conservative maximum, run representative traffic, and observe throughput, latency, waiting threads and database load. Increase or decrease capacity based on evidence, not a copied formula alone.

## Next steps

Keep the configuration small, record the exact library version or source revision, and test the complete application-to-database path. For broader topics, use the [HikariCP guide library](https://hikaricp.com/blog.html) or return to the [homepage FAQ](https://hikaricp.com/index.html#faq).",

      "title": "HikariCP Default Maximum Pool Size in Spring Boot: 10 Connections",
      "content": "**The default HikariCP maximum pool size is 10 database connections per HikariCP connection pool.** In Spring Boot, configure it with `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size`. The value is a ceiling for connections the pool can hold—not a guarantee that 10 connections are opened immediately.

HikariCP documents `maximumPoolSize` with a default value of **10**. It includes both idle and in-use connections in that pool. See the [HikariCP configuration documentation](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP).

For a conventional Spring Boot datasource, the corresponding property is:

`spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20`
That example raises the maximum from 10 to 20. The setting normally applies to each HikariCP pool, usually meaning each datasource in each running application instance.

Normally, no. HikariCP owns the documented default of 10, while Spring Boot commonly selects HikariCP when it is available and exposes its settings through the `spring.datasource.hikari` namespace. Spring Boot’s current [data-access documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-access.html) describes this configuration path.

Do not assume every Spring Boot application uses HikariCP. The effective pool may be different if HikariCP is absent, another pool is explicitly selected, the application defines its own `DataSource` bean, or a platform or custom starter overrides datasource configuration.

### application.properties

`spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=25`
### application.yaml

```
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 25
```
The underlying HikariCP API is:

```
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setMaximumPoolSize(25);
```
For Spring Boot’s auto-configured datasource, prefer the Spring Boot property rather than constructing `HikariConfig` manually. Hikari-specific properties belong under `spring.datasource.hikari`.

`maximumPoolSize=10` means the pool is allowed to hold up to 10 database connections, including connections currently borrowed by application code and connections sitting idle in the pool.

It does not mean:

- the application has exactly 10 connections at all times;
- 10 physical database sessions must exist at startup; or
- all 10 connections are actively executing queries.

Actual connection creation and usage depend on demand, initialization behavior, idle settings, and the HikariCP version and configuration.

## `maximumPoolSize` versus `minimumIdle`

HikariCP documents the default `minimumIdle` value as the same as `maximumPoolSize`. With otherwise untouched defaults, that means:

```
maximumPoolSize = 10
minimumIdle     = 10
```
This relationship is easy to confuse with a guarantee that 10 connections are created immediately. It is better understood as the configured maximum and idle target; actual creation still depends on pool behavior and application demand.

HikariCP’s documentation generally recommends not setting `minimumIdle` when you want the pool to operate as a fixed-size pool that can respond efficiently to traffic spikes. Follow the guidance for the HikariCP version used by your application.

When every connection is in use, a new caller waits for a connection to be returned. HikariCP allows that wait to continue up to `connectionTimeout`; if no connection becomes available, acquisition fails with a timeout. The documented behavior is described in the [HikariCP configuration reference](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP).

The common symptom chain is:

```
Pool reaches its maximum
        ↓
New callers wait for a connection
        ↓
Connection-acquisition latency rises
        ↓
Callers reach connectionTimeout
        ↓
The application reports pool or database timeout errors
```
A timeout does not prove that the database is unavailable or that the pool is simply too small. Other causes include slow queries, long transactions, connection leaks, database throttling, network problems, or code that holds a connection while performing non-database work.

There is no universal production value. Ten may be reasonable for a modest service, excessive for a small database, or insufficient for a genuinely database-bound workload. Increasing it blindly can make performance worse by adding database CPU and memory pressure, lock contention, I/O contention, context switching, and connection-establishment work.

Plan the deployment-wide connection budget rather than looking only at one configuration file:

```
Possible connections ≈ pool size per instance
                       × number of instances
                       × number of independent pools
```
This is a planning approximation, not a promise that all connections will be active simultaneously.

For example, 10 application instances with a maximum of 10 could potentially use up to 100 connections. If each instance has both a primary and read-only datasource, the potential total doubles again. Rolling deployments, blue/green releases, Kubernetes autoscaling, and serverless concurrency can temporarily multiply the number of pools.

### Inputs to consider

- **Database budget:** account for the database’s connection limit and reserve capacity for administration, monitoring, replication, migrations, and other services.
- **Deployment size:** include normal replicas, autoscaling limits, and overlapping old and new versions during deployments.
- **Number of pools:** count primary, read-replica, tenant-specific, reporting, and batch datasources separately.
- **Application concurrency:** measure how many requests are simultaneously waiting on database work.
- **Query and transaction duration:** long-running work keeps connections checked out longer and can exhaust a pool even when request volume is moderate.
- **Database capacity:** consider CPU, memory, I/O, locks, and the amount of parallel work the database can process efficiently.
- **Pool metrics:** examine active connections, idle connections, pending acquisition threads, acquisition latency, and timeout counts.

Application concurrency, database concurrency, and pool capacity are related but not interchangeable. A larger pool helps only when the pool is the bottleneck and the database has capacity for additional parallel work.

### Check configuration and overrides

Inspect the active configuration files and environment variables:

`SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUM_POOL_SIZE=20`
Spring Boot’s relaxed binding maps the canonical kebab-case property to this environment-variable form. Also verify the active profile, configuration location, and property precedence.

The canonical property is:

`spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20`
Common incorrect alternatives include:

```
spring.datasource.maximum-pool-size
spring.datasource.hikari.maximumPoolSize
spring.datasource.hikari.max-pool-size
```
### Identify the runtime datasource

Check startup logs, the dependency tree, the configured datasource type, or the runtime class. A Hikari-backed datasource commonly appears as:

`com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource`
If the application uses Tomcat JDBC, DBCP2, a vendor-specific pool, R2DBC, or a custom datasource, HikariCP’s default of 10 does not describe the effective pool.

### Inspect the runtime configuration

For a diagnostic check, you can inspect the actual datasource:

```
@Autowired
private DataSource dataSource;
@PostConstruct
void logPoolConfiguration() {
    if (dataSource instanceof HikariDataSource hikari) {
        logger.info("Hikari maximum pool size: {}",
                hikari.getMaximumPoolSize());
    }
}
```
Use structured logging or metrics rather than `System.out.println` in production. HikariCP also exposes configuration and management information through its APIs and, where enabled, JMX. The [HikariConfig API documentation](https://javadoc.io/static/com.zaxxer/HikariCP/7.0.2/com/zaxxer/hikari/HikariConfig.html) includes the getter and setter for this property.

### Use metrics carefully

With Spring Boot Actuator and Micrometer configured, datasource pool metrics can show active, idle, pending, and maximum capacity. Exact metric names and tags vary by Spring Boot, Micrometer, and registry versions, so verify the names exposed by the version in your application instead of assuming a universal path.

Hibernate settings such as JDBC batch size, fetch size, query behavior, and transaction handling do not normally change HikariCP’s `maximumPoolSize`. However, ORM and transaction behavior strongly affect how long connections remain checked out.

A Hibernate or JPA problem can therefore look like a pool-sizing problem. Inspect transaction boundaries, slow queries, lazy-loading behavior, and connection-handling behavior before increasing the pool. A transaction that holds a connection while making an HTTP request, performing file I/O, waiting on a message broker, or doing expensive CPU work can exhaust a pool regardless of whether the configured maximum is 10 or 50.

### “The pool is stuck at 10”

1. Confirm that the runtime datasource is actually `HikariDataSource`.
2. Inspect the effective `maximumPoolSize`, not just the source configuration.
3. Check active, idle, pending, and timeout metrics.
4. Inspect database sessions and long-running queries.
5. Review transaction duration and connection-return behavior.
6. Check for leaks, database throttling, locks, and network delays.
7. Verify the active Spring profile and environment-variable overrides.
8. Change the pool size only after confirming that pool capacity, rather than query or database performance, is the bottleneck.

### “I set the property but it had no effect”

Check the active configuration file and profile, environment-variable precedence, custom `DataSource` beans, explicit datasource type, and whether the application is using HikariCP at all. A custom datasource may require direct configuration through its own builder or API rather than `spring.datasource.hikari`.

### “Increasing the pool made the database slower”

The database may already have been at its useful parallelism limit. More connections can increase CPU or I/O saturation, lock contention, and context switching. Multiple replicas may also have multiplied the total connection count. In this situation, optimize queries and transaction boundaries, reduce unnecessary concurrency, or protect the database with a smaller pool rather than continuing to increase the maximum.

Each HikariCP datasource generally has its own pool and maximum. A primary datasource and a read-only datasource configured at 10 each can allow up to 20 connections per application instance. Tenant-specific or reporting pools add their own capacity to the total.

The exact property names for multiple datasources depend on how those datasources are bound and constructed. If they are custom-defined, configure each `HikariDataSource` or `HikariConfig` explicitly and verify each runtime pool independently.

For the conventional HikariCP setup in Spring Boot, the documented default `maximumPoolSize` is **10 connections per pool**. Spring Boot normally exposes it as `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size` without replacing HikariCP’s default. Treat 10 as a starting ceiling, calculate the total across instances and datasources, and use runtime metrics and database behavior—not an arbitrary formula—to choose a production value.",

      "content": "Fast, simple, reliable.  HikariCP is a "zero-overhead" production ready JDBC connection pool.  At roughly 165Kb, the library is very light.  Read about [how we do it here](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Down-the-Rabbit-Hole).

**"Simplicity is prerequisite for reliability."**

- *Dr. Edsger Dijkstra*

Important

In order to avoid a rare condition where the pool goes to zero and does not recover it is necessary to configure *TCP keepalive*. Some JDBC drivers support this via properties, for example `tcpKeepAlive=true` on PostgreSQL, but in any case it can also be configured at the OS-level. See [Setting OS TCP Keepalive](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Setting-Driver-or-OS-TCP-Keepalive) and/or [TCP keepalive for a better PostgreSQL experience](https://www.cybertec-postgresql.com/en/tcp-keepalive-for-a-better-postgresql-experience/#setting-tcp-keepalive-parameters-on-the-operating-system).

**Java 11+** maven artifact:


HikariCP comes with *sane* defaults that perform well in most deployments without additional tweaking. **Every property is optional, except for the "essentials" marked below.**

<sup>📎</sup> *HikariCP uses milliseconds for all time values.*

🚨 HikariCP relies on accurate timers for both performance and reliability. It is *imperative* that your server is synchronized with a time-source such as an NTP server. *Especially* if your server is running within a virtual machine.  Why? [Read more here](https://dba.stackexchange.com/a/171020). **Do not rely on hypervisor settings to "synchronize" the clock of the virtual machine. Configure time-source synchronization inside the virtual machine.**   If you come asking for support on an issue that turns out to be caused by lack time synchronization, you will be taunted publicly on Twitter.

🔤`dataSourceClassName`

This is the name of the `DataSource` class provided by the JDBC driver.  Consult the
documentation for your specific JDBC driver to get this class name, or see the [table](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP#popular-datasource-class-names) below.
Note XA data sources are not supported.  XA requires a real transaction manager like
[bitronix](https://github.com/bitronix/btm). Note that you do not need this property if you are using
`jdbcUrl` for "old-school" DriverManager-based JDBC driver configuration.
*Default: none*

*- or -*

🔤`jdbcUrl`

This property directs HikariCP to use "DriverManager-based" configuration.  We feel that DataSource-based
configuration (above) is superior for a variety of reasons (see below), but for many deployments there is
little significant difference.  **When using this property with "old" drivers, you may also need to set
the  `driverClassName` property, but try it first without.**  Note that if this property is used, you may
still use *DataSource* properties to configure your driver and is in fact recommended over driver parameters
specified in the URL itself.
*Default: none*

🔤`username`

This property sets the default authentication username used when obtaining *Connections* from
the underlying driver.  Note that for DataSources this works in a very deterministic fashion by
calling `DataSource.getConnection(*username*, password)` on the underlying DataSource.  However,
for Driver-based configurations, every driver is different.  In the case of Driver-based, HikariCP
will use this `username` property to set a `user` property in the `Properties` passed to the
driver's `DriverManager.getConnection(jdbcUrl, props)` call.  If this is not what you need,
skip this method entirely and call `addDataSourceProperty("username", ...)`, for example.
*Default: none*

🔤`password`

This property sets the default authentication password used when obtaining *Connections* from
the underlying driver. Note that for DataSources this works in a very deterministic fashion by
calling `DataSource.getConnection(username, *password*)` on the underlying DataSource.  However,
for Driver-based configurations, every driver is different.  In the case of Driver-based, HikariCP
will use this `password` property to set a `password` property in the `Properties` passed to the
driver's `DriverManager.getConnection(jdbcUrl, props)` call.  If this is not what you need,
skip this method entirely and call `addDataSourceProperty("pass", ...)`, for example.
*Default: none*

✅`autoCommit`

This property controls the default auto-commit behavior of connections returned from the pool.
It is a boolean value.
*Default: true*

⏳`connectionTimeout`

This property controls the maximum number of milliseconds that a client (that's you) will wait
for a connection from the pool.  If this time is exceeded without a connection becoming
available, a SQLException will be thrown.  Lowest acceptable connection timeout is 250 ms.
*Default: 30000 (30 seconds)*

⏳`idleTimeout`

This property controls the maximum amount of time that a connection is allowed to sit idle in the
pool.  **This setting only applies when `minimumIdle` is defined to be less than `maximumPoolSize`.**
Idle connections will *not* be retired once the pool reaches `minimumIdle` connections.  Whether a
connection is retired as idle or not is subject to a maximum variation of +30 seconds, and average
variation of +15 seconds.  A connection will never be retired as idle *before* this timeout.  A value
of 0 means that idle connections are never removed from the pool.  The minimum allowed value is 10000ms
(10 seconds).
*Default: 600000 (10 minutes)*

⏳`keepaliveTime`

This property controls how frequently HikariCP will attempt to keep a connection alive, in order to prevent
it from being timed out by the database or network infrastructure. This value must be less than the
`maxLifetime` value. A "keepalive" will only occur on an idle connection. When the time arrives for a "keepalive"
against a given connection, that connection will be removed from the pool, "pinged", and then returned to the
pool. The 'ping' is one of either: invocation of the JDBC4 `isValid()` method, or execution of the
`connectionTestQuery`. Typically, the duration out-of-the-pool should be measured in single digit milliseconds
or even sub-millisecond, and therefore should have little or no noticeable performance impact. The minimum
allowed value is 30000ms (30 seconds), but a value in the range of minutes is most desirable.
*Default: 120000 (2 minutes)*

⏳`maxLifetime`

This property controls the maximum lifetime of a connection in the pool.  An in-use connection will
never be retired, only when it is closed will it then be removed.  On a connection-by-connection
basis, minor negative attenuation is applied to avoid mass-extinction in the pool.  **We strongly recommend
setting this value, and it should be several seconds shorter than any database or infrastructure imposed
connection time limit.**  A value of 0 indicates no maximum lifetime (infinite lifetime), subject of
course to the `idleTimeout` setting.  The minimum allowed value is 30000ms (30 seconds).
*Default: 1800000 (30 minutes)*

🔤`connectionTestQuery`

**If your driver supports JDBC4 we strongly recommend not setting this property.** This is for
"legacy" drivers that do not support the JDBC4 `Connection.isValid() API`.  This is the query that
will be executed just before a connection is given to you from the pool to validate that the
connection to the database is still alive. *Again, try running the pool without this property,
HikariCP will log an error if your driver is not JDBC4 compliant to let you know.
Default: none*

🔢`minimumIdle`

This property controls the minimum number of *idle connections* that HikariCP tries to maintain
in the pool.  If the idle connections dip below this value and total connections in the pool are less than `maximumPoolSize`,
HikariCP will make a best effort to add additional connections quickly and efficiently.
However, for maximum performance and responsiveness to spike demands,
we recommend *not* setting this value and instead allowing HikariCP to act as a *fixed size* connection pool.
*Default: same as maximumPoolSize*

🔢`maximumPoolSize`

This property controls the maximum size that the pool is allowed to reach, including both
idle and in-use connections.  Basically this value will determine the maximum number of
actual connections to the database backend.  A reasonable value for this is best determined
by your execution environment.  When the pool reaches this size, and no idle connections are
available, calls to getConnection() will block for up to `connectionTimeout` milliseconds
before timing out.  Please read [about pool sizing](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing).
*Default: 10*

📈`metricRegistry`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container.  This property
allows you to specify an instance of a *Codahale/Dropwizard* `MetricRegistry` to be used by the
pool to record various metrics.  See the [Metrics](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Dropwizard-Metrics)
wiki page for details.
*Default: none*

📈`healthCheckRegistry`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container.  This property
allows you to specify an instance of a *Codahale/Dropwizard* `HealthCheckRegistry` to be used by the
pool to report current health information.  See the [Health Checks](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Dropwizard-HealthChecks)
wiki page for details.
*Default: none*

🔤`poolName`

This property represents a user-defined name for the connection pool and appears mainly
in logging and JMX management consoles to identify pools and pool configurations.
*Default: auto-generated*

⏳`initializationFailTimeout`

This property controls whether the pool will "fail fast" if the pool cannot be seeded with
an initial connection successfully.  Any positive number is taken to be the number of
milliseconds to attempt to acquire an initial connection; the application thread will be
blocked during this period.  If a connection cannot be acquired before this timeout occurs,
an exception will be thrown.  This timeout is applied *after* the `connectionTimeout`
period.  If the value is zero (0), HikariCP will attempt to obtain and validate a connection.
If a connection is obtained, but fails validation, an exception will be thrown and the pool
not started.  However, if a connection cannot be obtained, the pool will start, but later
efforts to obtain a connection may fail.  A value less than zero will bypass any initial
connection attempt, and the pool will start immediately while trying to obtain connections
in the background.  Consequently, later efforts to obtain a connection may fail.
*Default: 1*

❎`isolateInternalQueries`

This property determines whether HikariCP isolates internal pool queries, such as the
connection alive test, in their own transaction.  Since these are typically read-only
queries, it is rarely necessary to encapsulate them in their own transaction.  This
property only applies if `autoCommit` is disabled.
*Default: false*

❎`allowPoolSuspension`

This property controls whether the pool can be suspended and resumed through JMX.  This is
useful for certain failover automation scenarios.  When the pool is suspended, calls to
`getConnection()` will *not* timeout and will be held until the pool is resumed.
*Default: false*

❎`readOnly`

This property controls whether *Connections* obtained from the pool are in read-only mode by
default.  Note some databases do not support the concept of read-only mode, while others provide
query optimizations when the *Connection* is set to read-only.  Whether you need this property
or not will depend largely on your application and database.
*Default: false*

❎`registerMbeans`

This property controls whether or not JMX Management Beans ("MBeans") are registered or not.
*Default: false*

🔤`catalog`

This property sets the default *catalog* for databases that support the concept of catalogs.
If this property is not specified, the default catalog defined by the JDBC driver is used.
*Default: driver default*

🔤`connectionInitSql`

This property sets a SQL statement that will be executed after every new connection creation
before adding it to the pool. If this SQL is not valid or throws an exception, it will be
treated as a connection failure and the standard retry logic will be followed.
*Default: none*

🔤`driverClassName`

HikariCP will attempt to resolve a driver through the DriverManager based solely on the `jdbcUrl`,
but for some older drivers the `driverClassName` must also be specified.  Omit this property unless
you get an obvious error message indicating that the driver was not found.
*Default: none*

🔤`transactionIsolation`

This property controls the default transaction isolation level of connections returned from
the pool.  If this property is not specified, the default transaction isolation level defined
by the JDBC driver is used.  Only use this property if you have specific isolation requirements that are
common for all queries.  The value of this property is the constant name from the `Connection`
class such as `TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED`, `TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ`, etc.
*Default: driver default*

⏳`validationTimeout`

This property controls the maximum amount of time that a connection will be tested for aliveness.
This value must be less than the `connectionTimeout`.  Lowest acceptable validation timeout is 250 ms.
*Default: 5000*

⏳`leakDetectionThreshold`

This property controls the amount of time that a connection can be out of the pool before a
message is logged indicating a possible connection leak.  A value of 0 means leak detection
is disabled.  Lowest acceptable value for enabling leak detection is 2000 (2 seconds).
*Default: 0*

➡`dataSource`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container. This property
allows you to directly set the instance of the `DataSource` to be wrapped by the pool, rather than
having HikariCP construct it via reflection.  This can be useful in some dependency injection
frameworks. When this property is specified, the `dataSourceClassName` property and all
DataSource-specific properties will be ignored.
*Default: none*

🔤`schema`

This property sets the default *schema* for databases that support the concept of schemas.
If this property is not specified, the default schema defined by the JDBC driver is used.
*Default: driver default*

➡`threadFactory`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container. This property
allows you to set the instance of the `java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory` that will be used
for creating all threads used by the pool. It is needed in some restricted execution environments
where threads can only be created through a `ThreadFactory` provided by the application container.
*Default: none*

➡`scheduledExecutor`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container. This property
allows you to set the instance of the `java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService` that will
be used for various internally scheduled tasks.  If supplying HikariCP with a `ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor`
instance, it is recommended that `setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true)` is used.
*Default: none*

➡`exceptionOverride`

This property is only available via programmatic configuration or IoC container. This property
allows you to set an instance of a class, implementing the `com.zaxxer.hikari.SQLExceptionOverride`
interface, that will be called before a connection is evicted from the pool due to specific exception
conditions. Typically, when a `SQLException` is thrown, connections are evicted from the pool when
specific *SQLStates* or *ErrorCodes* are present. The `adjudicate()` method will be called on the
`SQLExceptionOverride` instance, which may return one of: `Override.CONTINUE_EVICT`.
`Override.DO_NOT_EVICT` or `Override.MUST_EVICT`. Except in very specific cases
`Override.CONTINUE_EVICT` should be returned, allowing the default evict/no-evict logic to execute.
*Default: none*

🔤`exceptionOverrideClassName`

This property allows you to specify the name of a user-supplied class implementing the
`com.zaxxer.hikari.SQLExceptionOverride` interface. An instance of the class will be instantiated
by the pool to adjudicate connection evictions. See the above property `exceptionOverride` for a
full description.
*Default: none*

HikariCP has plenty of "knobs" to turn as you can see above, but comparatively less than some other pools.
This is a design philosophy.  The HikariCP design aesthetic is Minimalism.  In keeping with the
*simple is better* or *less is more* design philosophy, some configuration axis are intentionally left out.

Many connection pools, including Apache DBCP, Vibur, c3p0 and others offer `PreparedStatement` caching.
HikariCP does not.  Why?

At the connection pool layer `PreparedStatements` can only be cached *per connection*.  If your application
has 250 commonly executed queries and a pool of 20 connections you are asking your database to hold on to
5000 query execution plans -- and similarly the pool must cache this many `PreparedStatements` and their
related graph of objects.

Most major database JDBC drivers already have a Statement cache that can be configured, including PostgreSQL,
Oracle, Derby, MySQL, DB2, and many others.  JDBC drivers are in a unique position to exploit database specific
features, and nearly all of the caching implementations are capable of sharing execution plans *across connections*.
This means that instead of 5000 statements in memory and associated execution plans, your 250 commonly executed
queries result in exactly 250 execution plans in the database.  Clever implementations do not even retain
`PreparedStatement` objects in memory at the driver-level but instead merely attach new instances to existing plan IDs.

Using a statement cache at the pooling layer is an [anti-pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-pattern),
and will negatively impact your application performance compared to driver-provided caches.

Like Statement caching, most major database vendors support statement logging through
properties of their own driver.  This includes Oracle, MySQL, Derby, MSSQL, and others.  Some
even support slow query logging.  For those few databases that do not support it, several options are available.
We have received [a report that p6spy works well](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/issues/57#issuecomment-354647631),
and also note the availability of [log4jdbc](https://github.com/arthurblake/log4jdbc) and [jdbcdslog-exp](https://code.google.com/p/jdbcdslog-exp/).

Please read the [Rapid Recovery Guide](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Rapid-Recovery) for details on how to configure your driver and system for proper recovery from database restart and network partition events.

HikariCP has several Java system properties that control various aspects of the pool. These properties are *unsupported*
for user manipulation. It is possible though unlikely that they may not exist in the future. This means: do not open an issue of any kind if you have modified these properties. *Pretend you never heard anything about "secret properties".*

| Property | Description | 
|---|---|
| `com.zaxxer.hikari.blockUntilFilled` | When this property is set `true` *and* `initializationFailTimeout` is greater than 1, the pool will block during start until completely filled. | 
| `com.zaxxer.hikari.enableRequestBoundaries` | When this property is set `true`, HikariCP will bracket connection acquisition and return with calls to `Connection.beginRequest()` and `Connection.endRequest()`. | 
| `com.zaxxer.hikari.housekeeping.period` | This property controls the frequency of the housekeeping thread, represented in milliseconds. Really, don't mess with this. | 
| `com.zaxxer.hikari.legacy.supportUserPassDataSourceOverride` | When this property is set `true`, HikariCP will support the legacy behavior of overriding the `getUsername()/getPassword()` methods on *HikariDataSource*. Preferred method is overriding `getCredentials()`. | 
| `com.zaxxer.hikari.useWeakReferences` | When this property is set `true` it will force HikariCP to use `WeakReference` objects in the `ConcurrentBag` internal collection ThreadLocals and prevent the use of our `FastList` class, all to avoid TomCat warnings during redeploy. | 

Either don't use these properties or take on full responsibility for the consequences.

You can use the `HikariConfig` class like so<sup>1</sup>:

```
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/simpsons");
config.setUsername("bart");
config.setPassword("51mp50n");
config.addDataSourceProperty("cachePrepStmts", "true");
config.addDataSourceProperty("prepStmtCacheSize", "250");
config.addDataSourceProperty("prepStmtCacheSqlLimit", "2048");
HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config);
```
<sup>1</sup> MySQL-specific example, DO NOT COPY VERBATIM.

or directly instantiate a `HikariDataSource` like so:

```
HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource();
ds.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/simpsons");
ds.setUsername("bart");
ds.setPassword("51mp50n");
...
```
or property file based:

```
// Examines both filesystem and classpath for .properties file
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig("/some/path/hikari.properties");
HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config);
```
Example property file:

```
dataSourceClassName=org.postgresql.ds.PGSimpleDataSource
dataSource.user=test
dataSource.password=test
dataSource.databaseName=mydb
dataSource.portNumber=5432
dataSource.serverName=localhost
```
or `java.util.Properties` based:

```
Properties props = new Properties();
props.setProperty("dataSourceClassName", "org.postgresql.ds.PGSimpleDataSource");
props.setProperty("dataSource.user", "test");
props.setProperty("dataSource.password", "test");
props.setProperty("dataSource.databaseName", "mydb");
props.put("dataSource.logWriter", new PrintWriter(System.out));
HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig(props);
HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(config);
```
There is also a System property available, `hikaricp.configurationFile`, that can be used to specify the
location of a properties file.  If you intend to use this option, construct a `HikariConfig` or `HikariDataSource`
instance using the default constructor and the properties file will be loaded.

We recommended using `dataSourceClassName` instead of `jdbcUrl`, but either is acceptable.  We'll say that again, *either is acceptable*.

⚠ *Note: Spring Boot auto-configuration users, you need to use `jdbcUrl`-based configuration.*
